title: Going deeper in one
hookLine: some teachers say to go deep in one way rather than sampling forever

lines: A TOUR CAN BECOME A HABIT.
cards: "Everywhere means nowhere." Seneca wrote that in a letter to his friend Lucilius, warning him against reading one book, then another, then another, and settling into none. This path has been a tour, and tours are good.
You've sat in a Zen hall and a Quaker meeting, counted the Omer, walked with the Stoics. But a tour can quietly become a habit of its own: always the next thing, never the same thing twice.
Seneca's warning lands near the end of the tour, with a question attached. At some point, do you stop visiting and start digging?

teach.b: Seneca's letter makes the case with pictures. A traveler always on the road ends up with many acquaintances and no real friends. Food that leaves the stomach as soon as it's eaten never nourishes the body.
A remedy changed every day never gets the chance to heal. His advice to Lucilius, in paraphrase: stay with a limited number of great writers and really digest them, rather than skimming everyone.
Then the line: "Everywhere means nowhere." Seneca isn't against reading widely. He reads other schools himself, and in the same letter he quotes Epicurus, whose school differed from his own.
The point is depth, not narrowness. Some teachers in very different traditions say something similar about practice.

teach.h: PAST THE PART WHERE IT'S NEW.
teach.b: Learn widely if you like, they say, but choose one way and stay with it long enough for it to change you, through the dull weeks and the dry months, past the part where it's new.
A practice tried for a week shows you its surface. A practice kept for years starts to show you yourself.

teach.h: NOT A CALL TO CHANGE FAITHS.
teach.b: This isn't a call to change your faith, or to adopt one. If you already have a tradition, going deeper may simply mean returning to its own prayers, texts or practices with more attention.
If you don't, it may mean choosing one practice from this tour, a sit, a walk, a nightly review, and keeping it. The image to hold is a well. Lots of shallow holes give you a damp field.
One well, dug patiently, reaches water.

how: In some traditions, a practitioner settles into one main practice, such as a daily prayer, a sitting meditation or a regular study, and keeps it for years under a teacher or within a community, while still reading and learning more widely.

games.q: what does “going deeper in one” mean?
o: giving up your own faith to adopt a stricter one
staying with one practice long past its newness
sampling every school of practice once, for variety

games.q: going deeper in one: tap the pairs.
p: never gets the chance to heal

s: Seneca told Lucilius to read only Stoics
in the same letter he quotes Epicurus, whose school differed from his own. the point is depth, not narrowness.
going deeper can mean returning to a tradition you already have
it may simply mean coming back to its own prayers, texts or practices with more attention.
a practice shows its depth in the first week
a week shows its surface. it takes staying past the part where it's new.

games.q: a month into your one practice, it's gone dull. a new method you heard about sounds exciting. what does Seneca's letter suggest?
o: switch to the new method right away.
stay with the one you chose, past the dull part.
do both, and a third, to keep it fresh.
games.why: a remedy changed every day never gets the chance to heal. depth comes from staying past the newness.

practice: Let the practices you've met drift past: sitting, walking, singing, reading, reviewing the day, praying, if you pray.

Don't choose the most exciting; notice which one you keep returning to, or which quietly helped, and let it stay while the others go by. Then picture keeping that one, the same way, at the same time, for a month.

wordCard.voice: Going deeper in one. Choosing one practice and staying with it past its newness, as Seneca advised staying with a few writers instead of skimming them all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one well, deep. A practice kept for years starts to show you yourself. Keep digging.
